Good morning @quipnetwork ☕️

I want to cover the quantum research concept that is simultaneously the most important unsolved engineering problem in the field and the reason why Quip's architecture matters more as hardware advances.

Quantum error correction. Specifically surface codes.

Here's the physics problem they're solving.

Quantum states are fragile. Any interaction with the environment introduces errors. A qubit that should be in state 0 flips to 1. A phase relationship that should be preserved gets corrupted. Decoherence accumulates errors faster than computation can complete.

Classical computers solve error correction simply. Copy the bit multiple times. Take a majority vote. If you have three copies and one flips you know which one is wrong.

Quantum mechanics forbids this approach entirely.

The no-cloning theorem which I covered earlier makes it physically impossible to copy an unknown quantum state. You cannot make redundant copies to vote on. The most intuitive classical error correction strategy is fundamentally unavailable to quantum systems.

Quantum error correction had to invent an entirely different approach.

Surface codes are the current leading solution. Instead of copying quantum information they encode it across a 2D lattice of physical qubits in a way that allows errors to be detected and corrected without ever directly measuring the quantum state being protected.

The mechanism is elegant. You measure correlations between neighboring qubits called syndrome measurements rather than the qubits themselves. Errors show up as anomalies in the correlation pattern. You can identify and correct the error without collapsing the quantum state you're computing with.

The cost is significant. Surface codes require roughly 1,000 physical qubits to protect one logical qubit at useful error rates. IBM's path to fault-tolerant quantum computation requires millions of physical qubits to run algorithms with thousands of logical qubits.

That's why fault-tolerant gate-based quantum computation is years away.

Google's Willow chip demonstrated something critical this year that surface code error rates decrease as you add more qubits rather than increasing. The scaling relationship that makes large-scale fault-tolerant computation physically achievable rather than theoretically possible.

That result moved timelines.

Here is the precise connection to @quipnetwork that I keep thinking about.

Every milestone in quantum error correction research better surface codes, higher distance codes, more efficient syndrome extraction moves the fault-tolerant threshold closer and does two things simultaneously for @quipnetwork :

First it accelerates the timeline for Shor's algorithm at scale. Post-quantum wallet infrastructure becomes more urgent.

Second it expands the class of problems gate-based quantum hardware can attack efficiently. The compute marketplace addressable market grows.

Both consequences increase @quipnetwork 's relevance.

D-Wave's annealing architecture sidesteps the surface code requirement by operating in a regime where partial decoherence tolerance is sufficient. That's why it's winning blocks today.

But as surface code implementations mature and gate-based hardware approaches fault tolerance the quantum compute landscape expands dramatically. More problem classes. More enterprise applications. More reasons to route workloads through a decentralized quantum marketplace rather than a centralized cloud.

My honest long view:

The quantum error correction research trajectory is the single most important technical development to follow if you want to understand the quantum computing timeline accurately.

Surface codes scaling correctly which Willow demonstrated is not an incremental improvement. It's the experimental confirmation that the path to fault-tolerant quantum computation is physically open.

The distance between here and fault-tolerant quantum computation just got measurably shorter.

China's Brain–Computer Interface revolution: BCI companies in China are growing at an incredible pace

In March 2026, China became the first country to approve an implantable brain–computer interface (BCI) device for commercial medical use.

The device, developed by Shanghai-based Neuracle Medical Technology, helps people with paralysis control a robotic glove using brain signals.

The US and Switzerland have also made progress with BCI technology, but their implantable systems are still in clinical trials.

China's efforts to build a commercial BCI industry are relatively recent, yet progress has been fast.

The number of BCI companies is growing rapidly:
Shanghai: 17 in 2024  60 in 2025
Guangdong: 80  100
Jiangsu: 37  55
Sichuan: 13  26

Shanghai saw the largest increase, with the number of firms more than tripling in just one year.

China now has more than 200 BCI firms, second only to the United States.
Source: @MERICS, CCID Consulting, @FudanUniversity
